chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) said: 'Do not shave the children in the manner of al-Qaza', and al-Qaza is that one shaves a part and leaves a part.'

key_terms.أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ: Amir al-Mu'minin (Commander of the Faithful, referring to Imam Ali)
key_terms.الْقَزَعَ: Al-Qaza (a specific style of partial shaving)

ai.seo_question: What is the definition of Al-Qaza in Islamic tradition regarding children's hair?
ai.summary: This hadith, recorded in Al-Kafi, traces the prohibition of 'Qaza' (partly shaven) back to Imam Ali (AS), linking the practice to pre-Islamic Jahiliyyah customs of partial shaving. In Shia jurisprudence, this is often interpreted as a rejection of imitating non-Muslim or pagan grooming styles, emphasizing uniformity and modesty in a child's appearance as a reflection of Islamic identity.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Al Nowfaly, from Al Sakuny, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup>
having said: ‘Amir Al-Momineen<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Do not shave off the children in the cracked (manner), and the cracked is that he is shaved in a place and left in a place’.
en.sarwar: 1. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from al-Nawfaliy from al-Sakuniy who has said the following: “Abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, has said that ’Amir al-Mu’minin has said, ’
Do not shave the heads of children in al-Qaza‘ and al-Qaza‘ meaning to shave certain parts and leave other parts.’”
